title: VIP:::FRCS:EMERGENCY MEDICINE FOR FRCS: STROKE & ENDOCRINE CRISES
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide for the FRCS (Glasg) Exam covering Acute Stroke, Intracranial Pressure, Diabetic Emergencies (DKA, HONK, Hypoglycemia), and Thyroid/Adrenal crises. Designed for rapid review of diagnostic pointers and management protocols.

sections.title: Stroke: Definition & Clinical Manifestation
sections.content: Definition: ischemic infarction (or bleeding into) any part of the brain. It manifests by rapid onset (over minutes) of focal CNS signs and symptoms (contralateral hemiplegia & sensory loss + homonymous hemianopia).

branches: CNS bleed (hypertension, trauma and aneurysm rupture)

sections.title: Risk Factors
content: Hypertension
Hypercholesterolemia
Smoking
DM
Heart disease (AF, valvular, ischaemic)

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Call for help.
2. A → Adequate ventilation.
3. B → Oxygenation.
4. C → Circulation → IV line.
5. Document Level of consciousness.
6. Vital sign monitoring: For hypertension, admit and control over days not hours.
7. Admission to stroke units for nursing/physio (saves lives and provides motivation).

rows: Within a few days to differentiate hemorrhagic from ischemic if considering anticoagulation.
Meningism, severe headache, and coma within hours.
Carotid bruit, AF, and past TIA.

content.explanation: NB1. TIA: sudden onset of focal CNS signs (resolve within few minutes) due to temporary occlusion, usually by emboli, of part of cerebral circulation. NB2: carotid bruit may signify stenosis (>30%), often near internal carotid origin. Best heard behind the angle of the jaw.

sections.title: Comprehensive Investigations List
content: FBC
CXR
ECG
ESR
U&E
Lipids
Blood glucose
Clotting tests
Echo
Carotid doppler
Carotid angiography

sections.title: Stroke Treatment Strategy
content: Aspirin: 300mg/24h PO (unless strong suspicion of CNS bleeding).
Nil by mouth if swallowing is a problem.
Maintain hydration: Do not over-hydrate (cerebral edema).
Monitor and treat ↑ BP.
Immediate evacuation: Refer if cerebellar hemorrhage is possible.
Nursing care: Turn regularly and keep dry (consider catheterization) to stop bed sores.
DVT Prophylaxis: Passive limb movements, subcutaneous heparin, and compressing stockings.
Support: Emotional support and rehabilitation.

sections.title: Thrombolysis & Prevention
content: NB Thrombolysis: Alteplase within 3h of onset may decrease adverse outcomes (trials). Requires dedicated 24h CNS thrombolysis teams. Note: Not yet recommended in the UK in 2016.
Prevention 1: Control risk factors.
Prevention 2: Exercise (↑ HDL).
Prevention 3: Life long anticoagulants for rheumatic/prosthetic heart valves on left side.
Prevention 4: Aspirin 75 mg/day for life.

sections.title: Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
content: Normal ICT: 0-10 mmHg.
Causes: Tumours (1ry or metastatic), Head injury, Brain haemorrhage (any type).
Causes: Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess), Hydrocephalus, Cerebral oedema, Status epilepticus.

sections.title: Signs & Symptoms of ICP
content: Headache, vomiting ± nausea.
Deterioration of consciousness: drowsiness, irritability, seizures, coma.
Cushing’s response: ↓ pulse, ↑ BP & Cheyne-Stokes respiration.
Ophthalmic: ↓ VA & peripheral visual field loss.
Ophthalmic: Pupil changes (constriction 1st, later dilatation). DON’T DILATE.
Papilloedema: Loss of previous spontaneous venous pulsation. (If preserved, exclude papilloedema).

sections.title: ICP Management
content: 1. ABC (Intubate if needed).
2. Correct hypotension & treat seizures.
3. Brief history & examination.
4. Elevate head of bed 30º- 40º.
5. Mannitol 20%: 1-2g/kg IV over 10-20 min (5mL/kg). Clinical effect after 20 min, lasts 2-6h. Aim for serum osmolarity 300 mosmol/kg.
6. Dexamethasone: 10 mg IV then 4 mg/6h IV/PO (if cerebral oedema).
7. Fluid restriction to < 1.5L/d.
8. Close monitoring of ICP & vitals.
9. Search for cause & treat factors like hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia.
10. Refer to neurosurgeon for definitive treatment.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Treatment
content: Give 200–300 mL of 10% dextrose IV (20-30g).
OR Glucagon 1mg IM (if no IV access; will not work in drunk patients).
Once conscious: give sugary drinks & a meal.
Thiamine 1-2 mg/kg IV: if malnutrition or alcohol suspicion.
If oral hypoglycemic history: Admission for 10% glucose over 1-2 hours.

sections.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
sections.content: DKA coma only occurs in type I D.M (IDDM); it may be the mode of presentation. Diagnosis requires: hyperglycaemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3).

sections.title: DKA: Signs & Precipitants
content: Signs: Gradual drowsiness, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, polydipsia, lethargy, anorexia, polyuria, ketotic breath, coma.
Precipitants: Infection, surgery, MI, chemotherapy, non-compliance, or wrong insulin dose.

sections.title: DKA Fluid Replacement Protocol
content: 1. IV 0.9% saline immediately (Dehydration correction is priority).
2. 1L stat.
3. 1L over next 1 hour.
4. 1L over next 2 hours.
5. 1L over next 4 hours.
6. 1L over next 6 hours.
7. Use Dextrose 5% when blood glucose is < 10 mmol/L.
8. Caution in elderly/heart failure; monitor CVP.

sections.title: DKA Insulin & Potassium Management
content: Insulin Pump: 50U soluble insulin in 50ml saline (1U/ml). Give 4-8 U/h if glucose > 20mmol/L. Aim for fall of 5 mmol/L per h.
If No Pump: Load 20U IM, then 4-6 U/h IM while glucose > 10mmol/L.
K+ Replacement: Add 20-40mmol/L to IV fluid (Normal K+: 3.5-5).
K+ Shifting: Serum K+ is high in DKA due to lack of insulin, but total body K+ is low. Insulin shifts K+ into cells; must monitor to prevent hypokalaemia/arrhythmias.
K+ Timing: Don't add to 1st bag. Start when urine flow > 30ml/h.

rows: Longer history (1 wk), glucose > 35 mmol/L, marked dehydration.
Focal CNS signs, DIC, DVT (fully heparinize).
Rehydration with 0.9% saline (1/2 DKA rate) over 48h. Heparinize.

sections.title: Hyperthyroid Crisis (Thyrotoxic Storm)
content: Signs: Hyperpyrexia (>41°C), Tachycardia (>140bpm), AF, CHF, Diarrhea, Vomiting, Agitation, Coma.
Precipitated by: Infection, trauma, MI, stroke, stopping antithyroid meds, surgery, radioiodine.
Propranolol: 40 mg/8h PO or 1 mg IV over 1min (unless asthma/heart failure).
Carbimazole: 15-25 mg/6h PO; followed by Lugol’s solution 0.3 mL/8h after 4h.
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/6h IV or Dexamethasone 4 mg/6h PO (blocks T4 to T3 conversion).
Aspirin Warning: Avoid Aspirin as it can ↑ T4.

sections.title: Myxoedema Coma
content: Signs: Hypothyroid, >65yrs, hypothermia, hyporeflexia, ↓ glucose, bradycardia, goitre, cyanosis.
Management: High flow O2, Correct hypoglycaemia.
T3: 5-20 ug/12h IV slowly (Caution: may precipitate ischaemia).
Hydrocortisone: 100 mg/8h IV if pituitary cause suspected.
Avoid precipitating LVF with saline.

sections.title: Addisonian & Hypopituitary Crisis
content: Addisonian: Endocrinal shock, hypoglycemia. Treat with Hydrocortisone 100mg/6h IV and IV fluids.
Hypopituitary: Refractory hypotension, short stature, loss of axillary/pubic hair, hypoglycaemia.
Hypopituitary Management: Hydrocortisone IV first, then Liothyronine (T3) 10 ug/12h PO. Surgery if pituitary apoplexy.

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
content: Definition: Rare catecholamine-producing tumour of adrenal medulla.
Signs: Pallor, pulsating headache, malignant hypertension, VT, cardiogenic shock.
Emergency Management: Phentolamine 2-5 mg IV (repeat to maintain safe BP).
Follow-up: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg/24h PO (titrate up to 30 mg).
Elective surgery usually performed after 4-6 weeks.
